concepts.name: Revenue System: Zabt (Measurement-based Assessment)
key_dimensions: Distinction between Zabt system vs. Batai (crop-sharing) and Nasaq methods used simultaneously
Role of Sher Shah as precursor to Akbar's Zabti system — similarities, differences, and who gets credit
Use of Sikandari Gaz (yard of measurement) and Bigha as standardized units — UPSC trap on continuity vs. innovation
Direct state-peasant relationship bypassing zamindars — administrative significance and comparison with Mughal practice

concepts.name: Land Revenue Rate and the 'One-Third' Principle
key_dimensions: Fixing revenue at one-third of produce — comparison with Alauddin Khalji's one-half and Akbar's one-third under Todar Mal
Distinction between assessed demand (jama) and actual collection (hasil) — UPSC trap on whether Sher Shah achieved full realization
Patta (title deed to peasant) and Qabuliyat (peasant's agreement) as twin instruments — institutional innovation
Whether the system was welfare-oriented or purely extractive — historiographical debate

concepts.name: Patta and Qabuliyat System
key_dimensions: Patta as a document issued TO the peasant vs. Qabuliyat as document issued BY the peasant — UPSC trap on direction of obligation
Legal enforceability and rights conferred on peasants under this system
Comparison with similar instruments under Akbar's reign — who institutionalized it more effectively
Significance in reducing arbitrary exaction by local revenue officials (amils)

concepts.name: Provincial Administration and the Iqta/Sarkar System
key_dimensions: Division of empire into Sarkars (districts) subdivided into Parganas — hierarchy and chain of command
Dual officials at Sarkar level: Shiqdar-i-Shiqdaran (military/executive) and Munsif-i-Munsifan (revenue/judicial) — UPSC trap on who did what
Elimination of hereditary Iqta assignments — shift toward salaried/transferable officials to prevent feudalization
Comparison with Delhi Sultanate Iqta system and Mughal Subah system — continuity and change

concepts.name: Pargana Administration: The Five Officials
key_dimensions: Five officials at Pargana level: Shiqdar, Amin, Fotadar, two Karkuns — specific roles and UPSC trap on overlapping functions
Bilingual record-keeping by Karkuns in Persian and Hindi (Devanagari) — significance for administrative reach and anti-corruption
Amin's role in revenue assessment vs. Shiqdar's role in law and order — distinction frequently tested
Pargana as the basic administrative unit — comparison with modern tehsil/taluk

concepts.name: Currency Reforms and the Silver Rupya
key_dimensions: Introduction of the silver Rupiya (180 grains) and copper Dam — Sher Shah as originator of the rupee, not the Mughals
Standardization of weight and purity — contrast with debased coinage of preceding period
UPSC trap: Akbar continued the rupee system — who 'established' it vs. who 'perfected' it
Ratio between Rupiya and Dam (1 Rupiya = 64 Dams under Sher Shah vs. changes under Akbar) — numismatic details

concepts.name: Road Network and the Grand Trunk Road
key_dimensions: Reconstruction and extension of Sadak-i-Azam (Sonargaon to Peshawar) — distinction from original Uttarapatha/Mauryan road
Infrastructure alongside roads: Sarai (rest houses) every 2 kos — dual function as administrative/intelligence posts
Postal relay (Dak Chowki) system using horses stationed at Sarais — comparison with Mongol Yam system
UPSC trap: GT Road as purely military vs. commercial and administrative multipurpose infrastructure

concepts.name: Sarai System: Administrative and Commercial Functions
key_dimensions: 1,700 Sarais built — numbers sometimes tested; distinction between Sarais for Hindus vs. Muslims within the same complex
Sarais as nodes of intelligence gathering, police outposts, and postal relay — not merely travellers' rest houses
Muqaddam and Chaukidar stationed at each Sarai — local accountability mechanism
Economic impact: standardization of weights and measures enforced at Sarais — link to commercial reforms

concepts.name: Military Administration and the Branding (Dagh) System
key_dimensions: Re-introduction of Alauddin Khalji's Dagh (branding of horses) and Chehra (descriptive rolls of soldiers) — UPSC trap on who originated vs. who revived
Purpose: preventing fraud of mustering ghost soldiers and substitution of inferior horses
Direct payment to soldiers bypassing intermediary commanders — link to Alauddin's precedent and contrast with Mughal mansabdari
Sher Shah's personal supervision of military musters — centralization of military control

concepts.name: Spy and Intelligence System
key_dimensions: Network of spies (barids) reporting directly to Sher Shah — parallel to Alauddin Khalji's and Firoz Shah's intelligence systems
Sarais doubling as intelligence posts — integration of infrastructure and surveillance
Officials' fear of reporting honestly vs. Sher Shah's insistence on accurate information — administrative culture
Comparison with Mughal intelligence under Akbar's Kotwal system

concepts.name: Judicial Administration and Sher Shah's Personal Justice
key_dimensions: Sher Shah as the final court of appeal — personal dispensation of justice as a legitimizing tool
Principle of equal justice regardless of rank — 'even if my own son committed murder' anecdote, its historiographical value
Munsif-i-Munsifan at Sarkar level as judicial officer — distinction from revenue and police functions
Absence of a separate codified legal system — reliance on Sharia and customary law, UPSC trap on limitations of the system

concepts.name: Trade and Customs Reforms: Abolition of Internal Tolls
key_dimensions: Abolition of multiple internal transit duties — goods taxed only at point of origin and point of sale (two points only)
Standardization of weights and measures across the empire — enforcement mechanism through Sarais
Impact on merchant class and market integration — comparison with Akbar's later trade policies
UPSC trap: Sher Shah's trade reforms as precursor to a unified market vs. Mughal continuation

concepts.name: Police Administration and the Muqaddam-Chaukidar System
key_dimensions: Village headman (Muqaddam) made responsible for crimes in his jurisdiction — collective village responsibility principle
Zamindars held co-responsible for dacoities in their area — shifting accountability to local power holders
Chaukidar as the lowest unit of police administration — continuity into British period
UPSC trap: Whether this was a welfare measure or a punitive/coercive control mechanism

concepts.name: Historiographical Debate: Sher Shah as Administrative Innovator vs. Synthesizer
key_dimensions: Argument that most of Sher Shah's reforms were revivals of Alauddin Khalji's measures — specific parallels (Dagh, Chehra, market control)
Argument that Sher Shah was Akbar's true precursor — which specific Mughal institutions trace directly to Sher Shah
Abbas Khan Sarwani's 'Tarikh-i-Sher Shahi' as primary source — its bias and limitations
UPSC trap: Attributing rupee, GT Road, and revenue reforms — who gets 'credit' in exam answers

concepts.name: Welfare Measures and Their Administrative Significance
key_dimensions: Hospitals (shifa khanas) and mosques built along roads — state welfare as legitimacy-building
Trees planted along GT Road for shade — Sher Shah's own reported statement about peasant welfare
Distinction between genuine welfare intent and administrative/political utility of these measures
Comparison with Firoz Shah Tughlaq's welfare works — similarities and key differences in scale and intent

concepts.name: Anti-Corruption Measures and Accountability of Officials
key_dimensions: Direct payment to peasants and soldiers to bypass middlemen — structural anti-corruption design
Dual bilingual record-keeping by Karkuns as a check against falsification
Transfer policy for officials to prevent entrenchment and local nexus formation
UPSC trap: Effectiveness of these measures — sources suggest widespread corruption persisted despite reforms

concepts.name: Sher Shah's Revenue Administration: Role of the Amin
key_dimensions: Amin as the key revenue assessment official at pargana level — distinct from Shiqdar's executive role
Amin's responsibility to personally measure land and assess crops — field-level implementation
UPSC trap: Amin vs. Munsif — different functions often confused in exam answers
Continuity of the Amin institution into Mughal revenue administration under different nomenclature

concepts.name: Sher Shah's Coins as Administrative Instruments
key_dimensions: Coins inscribed with both Persian and Devanagari script — symbolic inclusion and administrative reach to non-Persian speaking population
Standardized weight as a tool of market regulation — link between monetary and trade reforms
UPSC trap: The 'rupee' — Sher Shah's silver rupiya vs. later Mughal evolution; not to be confused with Muhammad bin Tughluq's token currency experiment
Copper Dam's role in everyday peasant transactions vs. silver Rupiya for larger commerce — two-tier currency system

concepts.name: Centralization vs. Decentralization: The Core Tension in Sher Shah's Administration
key_dimensions: Sher Shah's deliberate weakening of Afghan tribal chiefs (nobles) — breaking the Afghan confederacy model that caused Lodi downfall
Simultaneously empowering local village-level officials (Muqaddam, Chaukidar) — selective decentralization at the grassroots
UPSC trap: Was Sher Shah's administration truly centralized? — The short reign (1540–1545) meant full implementation was incomplete
Comparison with Akbar's centralization — Sher Shah as template vs. Akbar's more systematic execution
